justification_text:
My point estimates reflected a modestly bullish baseline for the S&P 500 across all three horizons, anchored around the 3050–3090 range. At the one-day horizon, I leaned on near-term momentum and the assumption that no major surprise catalysts were imminent, producing a tight estimate close to prevailing levels. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the target slightly higher to reflect a mild drift assumption consistent with the long-run upward bias in equities, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for scheduled macro data or Fed commentary to shift sentiment meaningfully. At the one-month horizon, the drift assumption continues to dominate, but I added a bit more upside to account for the compounding of that positive bias over roughly 21 trading days.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, realized volatility in equity markets tends to translate into roughly 0.5–1% daily moves under normal conditions, which justified a fairly tight band of about plus or minus 65 points. By one week, I widened the interval to reflect not just volatility scaling (roughly with the square root of time) but also the increased chance of encountering scheduled risk events like employment reports, inflation prints, or central bank statements. At one month, the interval widens substantially because a full month can contain multiple macro surprises, earnings guidance shifts, and geopolitical developments that are essentially unpredictable in advance.

There are several tail risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals in either direction. On the downside, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in economic data — particularly around labor markets or consumer spending — could trigger a reassessment of the earnings outlook and send prices well below 2820. A sudden credit event, a geopolitical escalation, or a hawkish policy surprise from the Federal Reserve could amplify that move significantly. On the upside, a decisive pivot signal from the Fed, a strong earnings season, or a resolution of a major macro uncertainty could drive a relief rally that blows through 3360 with relative ease.

It is also worth noting that the intervals themselves carry epistemic uncertainty — they represent my best attempt to characterize distributional uncertainty, but the true distribution of equity returns has fat tails that standard volatility-based frameworks tend to understate. Historically, monthly moves of 10–15% or more occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest, meaning the probability mass outside my stated intervals is likely somewhat higher than the implied 10% in aggregate.
